"Hand down" is a phrasal verb — a combination of a verb ("hand") and a particle ("down") that together create a new meaning. Like many phrasal verbs in English, it has more than one meaning, and each meaning is used in a different kind of situation. On top of that, there are two closely related forms — "hands down" and "hand-me-down" — that you absolutely need to know.
Meaning 1 — To Pass Something to the Next Generation

This is the most common and important meaning.

Core idea: When something is handed down, an older person gives it to a younger person, or one generation passes it to the next. The thing being passed can be a physical object, a skill, a story, a tradition, a belief, or knowledge.

Think of it visually: an elder is standing higher (in age, in authority, in time), and they reach down to pass something to someone younger. That image is where the phrase comes from.

Examples:

  • "This gold watch was handed down to me by my grandfather."
    His grandfather gave it to him; the watch has traveled through generations.
  • "The recipe for this bread has been handed down in our family for over 200 years."
    No one wrote it in a book they bought. It was taught and passed from parent to child, again and again.
  • "Our culture hands down its stories through songs, not books."
    The community passes its stories orally from elders to children.
  • "A love of reading was handed down to her by her mother."
    Not a physical thing, but a habit and a love — also something that can be handed down.

What can be "handed down"?

  • Physical objects: jewelry, tools, furniture, clothing, land
  • Knowledge and skills: recipes, farming methods, craftsmanship
  • Beliefs and values: religious faith, cultural traditions
  • Stories and history: family tales, folklore, legends

Grammar note:
You will most often see this in the passive voice — "it was handed down" — because the focus is on the thing being passed, not the person doing the passing. But the active form is also perfectly correct: "My grandmother handed down this ring to me."
Meaning 2 — To Officially Deliver a Ruling or Judgment

In formal and legal contexts, "hand down" means to officially announce or deliver a decision, verdict, ruling, or sentence. This is used when an authority — a judge, a court, a committee — makes a final, official decision.

Core idea: A judge sits physically above the courtroom on a raised bench. When they deliver a verdict, they are figuratively reaching down from their high position of authority to deliver judgment to the people below. So the decision is "handed down."

Examples:

  • "The judge handed down a sentence of five years in prison."
    The judge officially declared the punishment.
  • "The Supreme Court handed down its decision on Monday."
    The court officially announced its ruling.
  • "The committee handed down new guidelines for food safety."
    An authority issued official new rules.

Key point: This meaning is always used in formal, official situations. You would not use it in everyday casual conversation. If your friend makes a rule about where to sit at lunch, you would NOT say, "She handed down the seating rule." That would sound very strange. This meaning belongs in legal, governmental, or formal organizational contexts.

Now we come to a slightly different form: "hands down" (with an s on "hands"). This is used as an adverb or adjective phrase and it has a completely different meaning from the other two.

Core idea: "Hands down" means without any doubt, without any competition, easily, by far. You use it when something is so obviously the best (or worst, or biggest, etc.) that there is simply no argument about it.

Where does this come from?
This phrase originated in horse racing. When a jockey is so far ahead of all the other horses that victory is guaranteed, they can relax the reins and lower their hands — hands down — and still win effortlessly. So "hands down" came to mean an easy, undeniable victory or superiority.

Examples:

  • "She is hands down the best teacher I have ever had."
    No competition. No debate. She is clearly the best.
  • "That was hands down the most delicious meal I've eaten in years."
    The speaker is absolutely certain — there's nothing to compare it to.
  • "He won the race hands down."
    He won easily, without any difficulty.
  • "This is hands down the hardest exam I've ever taken."
    Not just hard — undeniably the hardest.

Important spelling note:

  • When used as an adverb/adjective phrase describing something: "hands down" (two separate words with an s)
  • "She is hands down the best." ✅
  • "She is hand down the best." ❌ (missing the s — this is a common mistake)
Meaning 4 — "Hand-Me-Down" (Something Passed From Older to Younger)

This is the noun and adjective form of Meaning 1, and it is extremely common in everyday English. A hand-me-down is something — almost always clothing, but sometimes toys, books, or other objects — that was originally owned by an older person and then given to a younger one, usually within a family.

Examples:

  • "These jeans are hand-me-downs from my older sister."
    The jeans were hers first. When she outgrew them, they were passed to her younger sibling.
  • "Growing up, I wore a lot of hand-me-downs because we didn't have much money."
    The family reused clothing across children to save money.
  • "He was tired of driving his brother's hand-me-down car."
    Here it's used as an adjective describing the car.

Spelling note: Always hyphenate it: hand-me-down. Not "hand me down" (three separate words) when used as a noun or adjective.
Comparing All the Forms Side by Side

Here's a quick mental map to keep them straight:

"hand down" (verb, two words) → to pass something across generations, OR to officially deliver a ruling.
"She handed down her wisdom to her students."
"The court handed down its verdict."

"hands down" (adverb/adjective, two words with an s) → without doubt; easily; clearly the best.
"This is hands down the best movie of the year."

"hand-me-down" (noun/adjective, hyphenated) → a second-hand item passed from an older person to a younger one.
"These are my brother's hand-me-downs."

Mistake 1: Writing "hand's down" with an apostrophe.
→ There is no apostrophe. It is simply hands down.

Mistake 2: Confusing "hand down" (pass between generations) with "hands down" (without doubt).
→ These are different phrases used in different situations. Notice the s.

Mistake 3: Using the legal meaning ("hand down a verdict") in casual situations.
→ Reserve this for formal, official contexts only.

Mistake 4: Forgetting the hyphen in "hand-me-down."
→ As a noun or adjective, it must be hyphenated.
A Quick Story to Remember It All

Maria's grandmother handed down her old sewing machine to her. It was a hand-me-down, worn and a little rusty, but it worked perfectly. Maria learned to sew on it and became incredibly skilled. She is hands down the best seamstress in her town. When a local dispute arose about whether traditional crafts should be taught in schools, the town council handed down a decision: yes, they must be.

In just a few sentences, all four uses appear naturally. That's "hand down" in all its forms.

FormMeaningExample
  • "hand down" as a verb = pass something to future generations, or officially deliver a judgment.
  • "hands down" as an adverb/adjective = without doubt; easily the best.
  • "hand-me-down" as a noun/adjective = a second-hand item passed from older to younger.

The common thread in all these meanings is the idea of something being given from above to below — from older to younger, from authority to the public, from a clear winner to those who never had a chance. Once you see that central image, the whole phrase clicks into place.
